secondaryCondition: Takotsubo cardiomyopathy (stress-induced apical ballooning syndrome with transient or residual left ventricular dysfunction, and its recurrence risk) in a veteran with service-connected post-traumatic stress disorder
secondaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.104, DC 7020 (cardiomyopathy), evaluated under the General Rating Formula for Diseases of the Heart by workload in metabolic equivalents: 100 percent when a workload of 3.0 METs or less produces symptoms of heart failure, 60 percent at 3.1 to 5.0 METs, 30 percent at 5.1 to 7.0 METs, and 10 percent when more than 7.0 METs produce symptoms. Because the acute ventricular dysfunction of takotsubo syndrome usually recovers within weeks, a compensable evaluation depends on documented residual or recurrent dysfunction rather than on the index event, and a fully recovered single episode with no residual workload limitation may leave the veteran service connected at 0 percent. Where a specific arrhythmic complication is documented it is rated under its own cardiovascular code rather than folded into the cardiomyopathy evaluation. Qualified-human rating review required
primaryCondition: Service-connected post-traumatic stress disorder, with a documented stressor and ongoing symptom severity sufficient to establish the diagnosis under the applicable diagnostic criteria
primaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.130, DC 9411 (posttraumatic stress disorder), rated under the General Rating Formula for Mental Disorders at 0, 10, 30, 50, 70 or 100 percent on the occupational and social impairment criteria. Qualified-human rating review required
etiologicalMechanism: Catecholamine-mediated myocardial stunning sequence, in which a psychiatric stressor supplies the trigger and the chronic post-traumatic stress disorder supplies both the exaggerated stress response and the recurrence pattern. Acute emotional or psychological stress activates the sympatho-adrenomedullary axis and discharges catecholamines; at the myocardial level, catecholamine excess produces the characteristic takotsubo pattern of apical and mid-ventricular akinesia with basal hyperkinesis through convergent mechanisms: an epinephrine-mediated switch of myocardial beta-adrenergic signalling from the stimulatory Gs pathway to the inhibitory Gi pathway, which is most pronounced at the apex where beta-receptor density is highest, so that catecholamine stimulation produces net negative inotropy rather than augmented contractility; catecholamine-mediated coronary microvascular spasm and endothelial dysfunction with impaired coronary flow reserve; intracellular calcium overload with contraction-band necrosis on histology; and oxidative stress with myocardial oedema visible on cardiac magnetic resonance. Chronic post-traumatic stress disorder is a plausible substrate for that response rather than a mere bystander, because the disorder is characterised by sympathetic hyperarousal, blunted parasympathetic or vagal tone and hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis dysregulation, so the catecholamine output for a given stressor is exaggerated, and because the disorder supplies recurrent stressor-linked exacerbations that can coincide with the cardiac event. Nayeri and colleagues (PMID 29544664) review the psychiatric literature on takotsubo cardiomyopathy and conclude that there is a strong association between pre-existing psychiatric illness, particularly anxiety and mood spectrum disorders, and takotsubo cardiomyopathy, and that acute exacerbation of psychiatric illness, rapid uptitration or overdose of certain psychotropic agents and electroconvulsive therapy may trigger it. Lazzeroni and colleagues (PMID 29168538) compared triggering events in 58 consecutive takotsubo syndrome patients with and without pre-existing anxiety disorders: 31 (53 percent) had a previous history of anxiety disorders, the rate of exclusively emotional triggering was higher in those with an anxiety disorder (74 versus 30 percent, p equals 0.001), and events with an undetermined trigger were more frequent in patients without an anxiety disorder (33 versus 10 percent, p equals 0.027), which is the closest located demonstration that a pre-existing psychiatric disorder biases the patient toward emotional triggering of the cardiac event rather than toward physically triggered disease. Gonuguntla and colleagues (PMID 38331372), using the National Inpatient Sample and National Readmission Database for 2016 to 2018, identified 23,220 takotsubo admissions of which 43.11 percent carried a psychiatric disorder, and found that the psychiatric-disorder group had a higher 30-day readmission rate (1.25, 95 percent confidence interval 1.06 to 1.47), more cardiogenic shock (adjusted odds ratio 7.3, 95 percent confidence interval 3.97 to 13.6), more mechanical ventilation (adjusted odds ratio 4.2, 95 percent confidence interval 2.4 to 7.5) and more cardiac arrest (adjusted odds ratio 2.6, 95 percent confidence interval 1.1 to 6.3) without increased mortality. That last study bears on residuals and recurrence rather than on causation, and the distinction matters. Framing under 38 CFR § 3.310: this is a § 3.310(a) proximate-result theory. The service-connected post-traumatic stress disorder is asserted to have proximately caused a separately rated cardiac disability, and the theory rests on the stressor-to-catecholamine-to-stunning sequence documented above plus a chronology in which the cardiac event occurs during or after the course of the service-connected psychiatric disease. It is not a § 3.310(b) aggravation theory unless the record shows pre-existing takotsubo syndrome or a pre-existing stress cardiomyopathy from a non-service-connected cause, in which case the baseline must be established and the natural progression deducted. One important boundary must be pleaded correctly and not concealed: where the proximate instrument was a psychotropic medication prescribed for the service-connected post-traumatic stress disorder and given in excess or rapidly uptitrated, the mechanism is treatment-mediated rather than disease-mediated, the correct label is a medication or treatment side effect under § 3.310(a), and the two theories should not be conflated in one opinion. Chronology and evidence sufficient for an examiner to conclude that the takotsubo cardiomyopathy is at least as likely as not caused by the service-connected post-traumatic stress disorder therefore require: (1) an established diagnosis of post-traumatic stress disorder with a documented stressor and current severity; (2) objective documentation of the cardiac event, which in practice means the characteristic apical ballooning or mid-ventricular wall-motion abnormality on ventriculography or echocardiography together with new electrocardiographic changes and troponin elevation and, in the ordinary case, coronary evaluation sufficient to exclude an acute coronary syndrome because the accepted diagnostic definitions of takotsubo syndrome require the absence of obstructive coronary disease or angiographic evidence of acute plaque rupture; (3) a temporal relationship between the event and a documented exacerbation of the psychiatric illness or a discrete stressor, rather than an event arising in the absence of any psychiatric correlate; (4) exclusion or weighing of the acute physical triggers that produce the same phenotype, which include sepsis, surgery and anaesthesia, pain, respiratory failure, subarachnoid haemorrhage, pheochromocytoma, cocaine or amphetamine use, chemotherapy and the peri-partum state; and (5) for a compensable evaluation, documented residual or recurrent left ventricular dysfunction because DC 7020 is rated by workload limitation. Three candid limitations belong on the face of the opinion. First, the located anchor literature measures psychiatric illness broadly, and its strongest signals come from anxiety and mood spectrum disorders; none of the three anchors measures post-traumatic stress disorder as the exposure and no post-traumatic-stress-disorder-specific takotsubo cohort was located, so the final step from psychiatric illness in general to this veteran's post-traumatic stress disorder is inferential and must rest on the individual record rather than on a study. Second, takotsubo syndrome is usually reversible, so many veterans with a legitimate causal theory receive a 0 percent evaluation and the opinion should say so rather than imply a compensable rating is automatic. Third, where the record shows a competing physical trigger of comparable timing, the equipoise is destroyed and § 3.102 cannot resolve the claim in the veteran's favour on causation alone. Rating discipline under § 4.14 prevents the same cardiac findings from being compensated twice, and no individual probability is asserted here.

medicalEvidence.title: Psychiatric Illness in Takotsubo (Stress) Cardiomyopathy: A Review.
medicalEvidence.authors: Nayeri A; Rafla-Yuan E; Krishnan S; Ziaeian B; Cadeiras M; McPherson JA; Wells QS
medicalEvidence.summary: Literature review concluding that there is a strong association between pre-existing psychiatric illness, particularly anxiety and mood spectrum disorders, and takotsubo cardiomyopathy, and that acute exacerbation of psychiatric illness, rapid uptitration or overdose of psychotropic agents and electroconvulsive therapy may trigger the syndrome. Supplies both the association and the exacerbation-trigger concept, while its own limitation — that the anchors are psychiatry-referral based and that further studies are needed — is why this row discloses that none of its anchors measures post-traumatic stress disorder as the exposure.

Evidence that a pre-existing psychiatric disorder biases the patient toward emotional rather than physical triggering of the cardiac event.

secondaryCondition: Meniere's disease (secondary endolymphatic hydrops with episodic vertigo, fluctuating sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus and aural fullness) following service-connected traumatic brain injury residuals
secondaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.87, DC 6205 (Meniere's syndrome (endolymphatic hydrops)): 100 percent for hearing impairment with attacks of vertigo and cerebellar gait occurring more than once weekly, with or without tinnitus; 60 percent for attacks occurring one to four times a month; 30 percent for attacks occurring less than once a month. Two rating points require qualified-human review: the interaction between DC 6205 and the separate evaluation of permanent hearing impairment under the hearing provisions of § 4.85, and the fact that DC 6205 is attack-frequency based, so a veteran with continuous imbalance but no discrete attacks does not satisfy it and must be evaluated under the appropriate neurologic or vestibular provision instead
primaryCondition: Service-connected residuals of traumatic brain injury, with a documented closed-head or blast injury and persistent physical residuals
primaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.124a, DC 8045 (residuals of traumatic brain injury), evaluated on its cognitive-impairment and subjective-symptom evaluation tables with separate evaluation of physical residuals in the affected body system. Note that § 3.310(d) supplies a presumption of proximate result for a closed list of traumatic-brain-injury sequelae — parkinsonism, unprovoked seizures, certain dementias, depression and diseases of hormone deficiency — and Meniere's syndrome is not on that list, so this row must proceed on individual causation evidence rather than on any presumption. Qualified-human rating review required
etiologicalMechanism: Otologic trauma sequence producing delayed endolymphatic hydrops. Trauma to the temporal bone and labyrinth can produce hydrops through several convergent pathways: direct injury to the membranous labyrinth and the endolymphatic duct or sac, with disruption of the longitudinal flow and resorptive capacity that normally maintain endolymph volume; labyrinthine concussion without fracture, in which the membranous labyrinth is injured by shearing forces against the bony capsule; fracture lines crossing or approaching the otic capsule with immediate or delayed leakage of perilymph and mixing of potassium-rich endolymph with perilymph, which is toxic to the cochlear and vestibular nerve endings; fibrotic obliteration or osteoneogenesis of the vestibular aqueduct, which can progress for weeks to years after the injury and progressively impair endolymph resorption; and rupture of Reissner's membrane with episodic potassium leakage, which reproduces the fluctuating hearing loss and episodic vertigo that define the syndrome. The result is a secondary, trauma-related endolymphatic hydrops that is clinically distinguishable from the idiopathic disease in that it has a recognised antecedent insult and, in some patients, a delayed onset after the injury. Paparella and Mancini (PMID 6877007) described 37 patients who developed Meniere's syndrome following acoustic (18) and physical (19) trauma and reported histopathologic characteristics in a patient who developed Meniere's syndrome after head trauma that appeared identical to idiopathic Meniere's disease, explicitly discussing cause-and-effect relationships and pathogenesis. Ferster and colleagues (PMID 28306649) reviewed secondary endolymphatic hydrops, reported that recent investigation has brought attention to traumatic and inflammatory insults as causes of it, and listed acoustic and mechanical trauma among the recognised etiologies with histopathological illustration. DiBiase and Arriaga (PMID 9386247) reviewed post-traumatic hydrops and state that post-traumatic Meniere's disease is a true clinical entity based on clinical observations and histopathologic study. Framing under 38 CFR § 3.310: this is a § 3.310(a) proximate-result theory, in which the service-connected traumatic brain injury residuals are asserted to have produced a separate, separately rated otologic condition at DC 6205. It is not a § 3.310(d) presumption case, because Meniere's syndrome does not appear on the closed list of sequelae that paragraph holds to be the proximate result of service-connected traumatic brain injury; the veteran must therefore carry the theory on individual medical evidence, and the opinion should say so rather than implying a presumption. It is equally not a § 3.310(b) aggravation theory unless the record shows pre-existing idiopathic Meniere's disease or pre-existing vestibular disease antedating the injury, in which case the baseline must be established by medical evidence created before the onset of aggravation or by the earliest evidence created between the onset of aggravation and the current evidence of severity, and the natural progression of the pre-existing disorder must be deducted. Chronology and evidence sufficient for an examiner to conclude that the Meniere's disease is at least as likely as not caused by the service-connected traumatic brain injury residuals therefore require: (1) a documented traumatic brain injury with the mechanism and severity described, including whether there was temporal bone or mastoid trauma, blast exposure or loss of consciousness; (2) audiometric documentation of fluctuating sensorineural hearing loss with the low-frequency predominance typical of hydrops, together with vestibular testing and, where available, electrocochleography or delayed-contrast magnetic resonance imaging of the inner ear; (3) an interval that makes sense in one of the two recognised patterns, either symptom onset in the period immediately after the injury or a delayed onset months to years after it, in which case the delay must be explained by the fibro-osseous and resorptive mechanism rather than left unaddressed; and (4) exclusion or weighing of the competing etiologies below. Four candid limitations belong on the face of the opinion. First, the anchor tier is descriptive rather than quantitative: the located evidence is a case series with histopathology and two clinicopathologic reviews, there is no population-level incidence estimate for post-traumatic hydrops, and no numeric probability may therefore be asserted in support of an individual claim. Second, Meniere's disease is idiopathic in the great majority of patients, so the diagnostic burden falls on the record establishing both the traumatic insult and its temporal relationship to the onset of the attacks; onset decades after the injury, or bilateral disease, weakens the nexus considerably. Third, traumatic brain injury itself produces dizziness, imbalance, tinnitus and post-traumatic headache, so a claim must show discrete episodic vertigo attacks satisfying the schedule's frequency tiers rather than continuous disequilibrium, and the rating discipline of § 4.14 requires that the same vestibular findings not be compensated once under DC 8045 and again under DC 6205. Fourth, the competing causes that must be excluded or weighed are idiopathic Meniere's disease, acoustic trauma or noise exposure, otosclerosis, perilymph fistula, vestibular migraine, benign paroxysmal positional vertigo, vestibular schwannoma, superior semicircular canal dehiscence, autoimmune inner ear disease, ototoxic medication exposure, syphilis and other infectious labyrinthitis, and prior otologic surgery. No individual probability is asserted here; § 3.102 governs and the opinion must rest on documented chronology, accounted-for competing causes and an approximate balance of evidence.

medicalEvidence.title: Trauma and Meniere's syndrome.
medicalEvidence.summary: Case series describing 37 patients who developed Meniere's syndrome following acoustic (18) and physical (19) trauma, with histopathologic characteristics appearing identical to idiopathic Meniere's disease in a patient who developed the syndrome after head trauma, and an explicit discussion of cause-and-effect relationships and pathogenesis. This is the strongest located clinical anchor for the proposition that physical trauma to the head can produce the Meniere's phenotype.

medicalEvidence.title: Secondary Endolymphatic Hydrops.
medicalEvidence.authors: Ferster APO; Cureoglu S; Keskin N; Paparella MM; Isildak H
medicalEvidence.summary: Review of secondary endolymphatic hydrops reporting that recent investigation has drawn attention to traumatic and inflammatory insults as causes, listing acoustic and mechanical trauma among the recognised etiologies alongside post-surgical inner ear effects, otosclerosis, medications and systemic inflammatory processes, with histopathological illustration of the mechanisms. Supplies the mechanistic anchor — trauma as a cause of hydrops rather than a coincidence — while its own limitation, that it is a literature review without a risk estimate, is disclosed in the row's text.

medicalEvidence.title: Post-traumatic hydrops.
medicalEvidence.summary: Review of post-traumatic hydrops stating that post-traumatic Meniere's disease is a true clinical entity based on clinical observations and histopathologic study, and that the traumatic insult may be a blow to the head or other acoustic or physical injury. Supplies the clinical-entity recognition that supports treating post-traumatic hydrops as a discrete diagnosis rather than as idiopathic Meniere's disease with an incidental injury history.

secondaryCondition: Myositis (statin-associated immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy with anti-HMGCR autoantibodies, presenting as symmetric proximal weakness with marked creatine kinase elevation and requiring immunosuppression) in a veteran on statin therapy prescribed for service-connected hypertension
secondaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.71a, DC 5021 (myositis), with the note to DCs 5013 through 5024 directing that group to be evaluated as degenerative arthritis on limitation of motion of the affected parts; because this disease presents predominantly as proximal muscle weakness with fatigue, falls and difficulty rising rather than as joint limitation, the applicable evaluation frequently requires a clinically justified analogous rating under §§ 4.20 and 4.27, and the § 4.56 criteria and § 4.59 guidance on painful motion govern where motion is relatively preserved. No diagnostic code is invented here; DC 5021 is the code the schedule provides for myositis. Qualified-human rating review required
primaryCondition: Service-connected hypertensive vascular disease (hypertension) for which a statin was prescribed as part of cardiovascular risk management, with the prescribing indication documented in the medication record
primaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.104, DC 7101 (hypertensive vascular disease; hypertension and isolated systolic hypertension), confirmed by readings taken on at least three different days and rated on the documented diastolic and systolic thresholds. Qualified-human rating review required
etiologicalMechanism: Pharmacological trigger of sustained autoimmunity, not a self-limited toxic myopathy. Statins inhibit 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-coenzyme A reductase, the rate-limiting enzyme of cholesterol synthesis, and the same inhibition up-regulates expression of the enzyme protein itself in regenerating skeletal muscle. In genetically susceptible patients that up-regulated enzyme becomes the antigenic target of an autoantibody response, and anti-HMGCR antibodies in turn drive an immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy in which the myofibres are destroyed by immune attack rather than by the direct toxic effect of the drug. The critical mechanistic feature for causation, and the reason this entity behaves differently from ordinary statin myalgia, is that regenerating muscle cells express high levels of HMGCR, so the antigen supply persists and the immune response can be sustained even after the statin is discontinued — which is why the disease requires immunosuppression rather than mere withdrawal. Mammen and colleagues (PMID 21360500) demonstrated that statin exposure induces expression of the target autoantigen in cultured cells, identified HMGCR as the autoantigen, showed that HMGCR expression is up-regulated in muscle biopsy tissue from anti-HMGCR-positive patients in cells expressing neural cell adhesion molecule as a marker of muscle regeneration, found anti-HMGCR autoantibodies in 45 of 750 patients presenting to a myositis centre (6 percent) of whom 92.3 percent of those aged 50 or older had taken statins, and concluded that the findings demonstrate a mechanistic link between an environmental trigger and the development of sustained autoimmunity. Nazir and colleagues (PMID 28277343), a systematic review of 100 published cases, found a mean age of onset of 64.72 years with 54.44 percent male, symmetric proximal muscle weakness as the main presenting feature in 83.33 percent of patients, a mean creatine kinase of 6,853 international units per litre, anti-HMGCR antibody positivity in all cases tested (57 of 57), necrosis or necrosis with inflammation on muscle biopsy in the great majority, a requirement for two or more immunosuppressants in 83.82 percent of patients to induce remission, resolution of symptoms in 91 percent after treatment, and unsuccessful statin rechallenge in most cases. Khoo and colleagues (PMID 40347460) identified 109 anti-HMGCR immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy cases across four cohorts, calculated a mean annual incidence of 2.9 cases per million person-years overall but 20.4 and 24.1 cases per million statin users per year in the United Kingdom and Australian cohorts, found that 101 of the 109 patients were statin-exposed with a median statin duration before diagnosis of three years and a range of one month to 23 years, that 8 patients (7.5 percent) were statin-naive, that median peak creatine kinase was 7,020 international units per litre, and that at follow-up fewer than half had normal creatine kinase (47.6 percent) or normal muscle power (46.2 percent), which underlines the refractory nature of the disease. Framing under 38 CFR § 3.310: this is a § 3.310(a) proximate-result theory carried through treatment, because the statin was prescribed to manage the service-connected hypertension and a disability that is proximately due to or the result of treatment required by a service-connected disease is itself service connected. It is not a § 3.310(b) aggravation theory unless the record shows pre-existing myopathy or a pre-existing immune-mediated disease antedating the statin course, in which case the baseline level of severity must be established and the natural progression of the pre-existing disorder deducted. Chronology and evidence sufficient for an examiner to conclude that the myositis is at least as likely as not caused by the statin prescribed for the service-connected hypertension therefore require: (1) documentation of the statin exposure with the specific agent, dose, start date and duration taken from pharmacy records; (2) documentation that the service-connected hypertension was the indication for which the statin was prescribed, because if the statin was prescribed for a non-service-connected indication the treatment-mediated chain to the service-connected disease is broken; (3) the antibody and tissue findings that define the entity, that is, positive anti-HMGCR antibody testing and, where available, muscle biopsy showing necrotizing myopathy, together with the creatine kinase level; (4) a temporal pattern of symptom onset during statin therapy rather than before it, with attention to the fact that onset may occur months to years after the first dose; and (5) persistence or progression after statin discontinuation, which is the clinical feature that distinguishes this immune-mediated disease from self-limited statin toxic myopathy and which therefore does the heaviest evidentiary work in the claim. Four candid limitations belong on the face of the opinion. First, 8 of 109 patients in the largest located cohort were statin-naive and the entity can occur without any statin exposure, so statin exposure is a trigger and not a sufficient condition; the diagnosis must rest on the antibody and biopsy findings rather than on the medication history alone. Second, the latency is long and variable — median three years with a range from one month to 23 years — so neither a long exposure nor a short one is exculpatory, and an examiner must not reason that a brief course excludes causation or that a long course proves it. Third, the competing causes that must be excluded or weighed include statin-associated self-limited toxic myopathy, hypothyroid and hyperthyroid myopathy, hypokalaemia and other electrolyte myopathies, polymyositis and dermatomyositis, inclusion body myositis, muscular dystrophies including limb-girdle and dysferlinopathy, malignancy-associated necrotizing myopathy, HIV and hepatitis-related myopathy, and other drug-induced myopathies such as those from colchicine, glucocorticoids and fibrates; several of these produce proximal weakness and elevated creatine kinase and are distinguished by antibody testing, biopsy and electromyography rather than by clinical impression. Fourth, rating discipline under § 4.14 and the note to DCs 5013 through 5024 prevent the same muscle weakness from being compensated twice, and where more than one evaluation is warranted within the musculoskeletal system the schedule requires a single evaluation reflecting the predominant disability picture. No individual probability is asserted here; § 3.102 governs and the opinion must rest on documented chronology, accounted-for competing causes and an approximate balance of evidence.

medicalEvidence.title: Autoantibodies against 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-coenzyme A reductase in patients with statin-associated autoimmune myopathy.
medicalEvidence.authors: Mammen AL; Chung T; Christopher-Stine L; Rosen P; Rosen A; Doering KR; Casciola-Rosen LA
medicalEvidence.summary: Identified HMGCR as the autoantigen in statin-associated immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy, showed that statin exposure induces expression of the target autoantigen, showed HMGCR up-regulation in regenerating muscle cells of anti-HMGCR-positive patients, found anti-HMGCR antibodies in 45 of 750 myositis-centre patients (6 percent) with 92.3 percent of those aged 50 or older having taken statins, and concluded that the work demonstrates a mechanistic link between an environmental trigger and the development of sustained autoimmunity. This is the causal-mechanism anchor for the row.

secondaryCondition: Dry eye syndrome (keratoconjunctivitis sicca and thyroid-eye-disease-associated ocular surface disease, with burning, foreign-body sensation, photophobia, fluctuating vision and risk of corneal epithelial breakdown) in a veteran with service-connected hyperthyroidism including Graves' disease
secondaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.79 contains no diagnostic code dedicated to dry eye syndrome or keratoconjunctivitis sicca. A clinically justified analogous evaluation under §§ 4.20 and 4.27 is therefore required, and the codes most commonly used for this disability are DC 6025 (disorders of the lacrimal apparatus (epiphora, dacryocystitis, etc.)), rated 20 percent bilateral and 10 percent unilateral, and DC 6018 (chronic conjunctivitis) where the predominant findings are conjunctival; where punctate corneal epithelial disease is documented, a keratopathy-based analogy may be considered on the actual findings. The code must follow the documented findings and not the diagnostic label, and no diagnostic code is invented here. Qualified-human rating review required
primaryCondition: Service-connected hyperthyroidism, including Graves' disease, with documented thyrotoxicosis and, where available, thyroid-stimulating-hormone-receptor antibody positivity or clinical thyroid eye disease
primaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.119, DC 7900 (hyperthyroidism, including, but not limited to, Graves' disease), which assigns 30 percent for six months after initial diagnosis and thereafter evaluates residuals of the disease and complications of medical treatment; the initial 30-percent period is not a permanent evaluation, and the secondary ocular surface disease is separately rated rather than folded into the thyroid evaluation. Qualified-human rating review required
etiologicalMechanism: Autoimmune orbital and lacrimal-gland sequence, with both a functional secretory component and a mechanical exposure component. In Graves' disease the thyrotropin-receptor-directed autoimmune process does not remain confined to the thyroid: orbital fibroblasts and preadipocytes share the target antigen and respond to it by proliferating, differentiating into adipocytes and secreting glycosaminoglycans, which expand the orbital tissues and produce proptosis, periorbital oedema, lid retraction and extraocular muscle enlargement. Two consequences converge on the ocular surface. The functional pathway is immune-mediated lacrimal gland dysfunction: the same inflammatory cytokine milieu that drives the orbit — including interleukin-6, tumour necrosis factor alpha and interleukin-17 — suppresses aqueous tear production and alters tear composition, so the tear film becomes unstable even in patients whose globes are not markedly proptosed, and ocular surface inflammation then becomes self-perpetuating as the compromised tear film fails to dilute and clear inflammatory mediators. The mechanical pathway is exposure: proptosis, lid retraction, an increased palpebral aperture, lagophthalmos and incomplete or infrequent blinking increase evaporative tear loss and expose the inferior cornea, which compounds the secretory deficit and can progress to punctate epithelial erosions, filamentary keratitis and, in severe cases, corneal ulceration. The resulting keratoconjunctivitis sicca is therefore a disease of the same autoimmune process rather than an unrelated sicca syndrome. Selter and colleagues (PMID 25584018) reviewed the literature and concluded that a close relationship exists between dry eye syndrome and Graves' ophthalmopathy, with mechanical impairment of orbital muscles and immune-mediated lacrimal gland dysfunction as the causes of dry eye in these patients. Rana and colleagues (PMID 35167950) reviewed ocular surface disease in thyroid eye disease and reported a paradigm shift away from the purely anatomical explanation, stating that a growing body of research indicates that ocular surface inflammation and multi-factorial changes to the homeostasis of the ocular surface contribute substantially to the ocular surface disease seen in these patients, in addition to anatomical changes such as proptosis and corneal exposure. McAlinden (PMID 26605355) provides the disease overview, describing thyroid eye disease as a complex orbital inflammatory disease that can be sight threatening, debilitating and disfiguring, and covering its epidemiology, risk factors, pathogenesis, presentation, clinical features, investigations and treatment. Framing under 38 CFR § 3.310: this is a § 3.310(a) proximate-result theory in which the service-connected thyroid disease is asserted to have produced a separate, separately rated ocular disability. It is not a § 3.310(b) aggravation theory unless the record shows pre-existing dry eye syndrome from a non-service-connected cause — for example long-standing aqueous-deficient dry eye from Sjögren's syndrome, blepharitis or medication — antedating the thyroid disease, in which case the baseline must be established by medical evidence created before the onset of aggravation or by the earliest evidence created between the onset of aggravation and the current evidence of severity, and the natural progression of the pre-existing disorder must be deducted. Chronology and evidence sufficient for an examiner to conclude that the dry eye syndrome is at least as likely as not caused by the service-connected hyperthyroidism therefore require: (1) a documented diagnosis of Graves' disease or hyperthyroidism with the supporting laboratory and clinical findings; (2) objective ocular surface testing rather than symptoms alone, that is, tear break-up time, Schirmer testing, ocular surface staining scores and, where recorded, meibomian gland assessment, together with the clinical description of proptosis, lid retraction, lagophthalmos or exposure; (3) a temporal relationship in which the ocular surface symptoms begin with or after the thyroid disease rather than before it; and (4) documentation of whether thyroid eye disease is active or quiescent and whether the veteran has received radioiodine, because the orbital disease can progress independently of the thyroid hormone level and can worsen after radioiodine ablation, which affects how the chronology is read. Four candid limitations belong on the face of the opinion. First, dry eye syndrome is extremely common in the general population and rises with age, so an opinion that does not exclude the ordinary causes cannot rise above mere possibility; those competing causes include aqueous-deficient disease from Sjögren's syndrome and other autoimmune disease, age-related lacrimal insufficiency, meibomian gland dysfunction and blepharitis, contact lens wear, computer and screen use, and the large class of medications that reduce tear production or alter the tear film, including antihistamines, tricyclic antidepressants, selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, diuretics, beta-blockers, isotretinoin and ophthalmic preserved drops. Second, symptom-based diagnosis alone is inadequate in an ocular surface claim because symptoms correlate poorly with signs, which is why objective testing is required above. Third, there is no dedicated diagnostic code for this disability, so evaluation proceeds by analogy under §§ 4.20 and 4.27 and the veteran should not be told a fixed rating attaches to the diagnosis; the analogous code follows the findings, and a veteran whose findings are predominantly lacrimal or conjunctival will be rated under a different analogy than one with corneal epithelial disease. Fourth, rating discipline under § 4.14 prevents the same ocular findings from being compensated twice, and any visual-field, motility or diplopia impairment produced by thyroid eye disease is evaluated under its own provisions rather than as part of the dry eye rating. No individual probability is asserted here; § 3.102 governs and the opinion must rest on documented chronology, accounted-for competing causes and an approximate balance of evidence.

medicalEvidence.title: The relationship between Graves' ophthalmopathy and dry eye syndrome.
medicalEvidence.authors: Selter JH; Gire AI; Sikder S
medicalEvidence.summary: Literature review of 55 papers, excluding case reports, concluding that a close relationship exists between dry eye syndrome and Graves' ophthalmopathy and identifying mechanical impairment of orbital muscles and immune-mediated lacrimal gland dysfunction as the causes of dry eye in these patients. Supplies both halves of the asserted mechanism — the mechanical exposure component and the secretory immune component.

medicalEvidence.title: Ocular surface disease in thyroid eye disease: A narrative review.
medicalEvidence.authors: Rana HS; Akella SS; Clabeaux CE; Skurski ZP; Aakalu VK
medicalEvidence.summary: Narrative review reporting a paradigm shift: ocular surface disease in thyroid eye disease has traditionally been attributed to anatomical changes such as proptosis and corneal exposure, but a growing body of research indicates that ocular surface inflammation and multi-factorial changes to ocular surface homeostasis contribute substantially. Supports rating the dry eye as a disease of the thyroid process rather than as an incidental age-related finding.

medicalEvidence.title: An overview of thyroid eye disease.
medicalEvidence.summary: Overview describing thyroid eye disease, also known as Graves' ophthalmopathy, as a complex orbital inflammatory disease that can be sight threatening, debilitating and disfiguring, and covering its epidemiology, risk factors, pathogenesis, presentation, clinical features, investigations and treatment. Provides the disease-level frame that makes the ocular surface findings part of the thyroid orbitopathy spectrum.

secondaryCondition: Chronic spontaneous urticaria exacerbated by nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug therapy (NSAID-exacerbated cutaneous disease, with increased wheal and angioedema burden over the pre-existing baseline) in a veteran receiving NSAIDs for service-connected osteoarthritis
secondaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.118, DC 7825 (chronic urticaria), which for the purposes of that code defines chronic urticaria as continuous urticaria occurring at least twice weekly, off treatment, for a period of six weeks or more, and provides treatment-based tiers at approximately 10, 30 and 60 percent depending on the frequency of episodes, the need for continuous systemic therapy and refractoriness to treatment. Two rating points require qualified-human review: the six-week off-treatment frequency requirement must be documented from the historical record rather than by stopping necessary therapy, and a single acute drug eruption does not satisfy the schedule definition and must not be labelled chronic urticaria on that basis. Where the urticaria is genuinely new rather than pre-existing, the correct rating route is the urticaria code applied to a de novo reaction and the theory changes as described below
primaryCondition: Service-connected osteoarthritis for which a documented COX-1-inhibiting nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug was prescribed or was used as directed
primaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.71a, DC 5003 (degenerative arthritis other than post-traumatic), generally evaluated through the affected joint's limitation-of-motion code, with the exact joint code determined by the actual anatomical site and findings; no joint code is selected here because no joint findings are assumed. Qualified-human rating review required
etiologicalMechanism: Pharmacologically mediated aggravation of an existing skin disease, not creation of the underlying disease. NSAID-exacerbated cutaneous disease occurs in a patient who already has chronic spontaneous or recurrent urticaria and who develops additional wheals, deeper swelling or angioedema after taking a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug that inhibits cyclooxygenase-1. The proposed mechanism is cross-reactive rather than immunologically specific: inhibition of cyclooxygenase-1 removes prostaglandin E2-mediated restraint on mast cells and shifts arachidonic acid metabolism toward the 5-lipoxygenase pathway, increasing cysteinyl leukotriene and other pro-inflammatory mediator availability, which in a patient whose mast cells are already primed by the underlying urticaria lowers the threshold for degranulation and increases cutaneous vascular permeability, producing a measurable increase in wheal and angioedema burden. Romano and colleagues (PMID 40837856), in a World Allergy Organization statement revising the classification and routine diagnosis of NSAID hypersensitivity, classify immediate or acute NSAID hypersensitivity reactions into four clinical types including NSAID-exacerbated cutaneous disease and distinguish that phenotype from NSAID-induced reactions occurring without underlying chronic urticaria and from single-drug immunoglobulin-E-mediated allergy; the statement also cautions that its diagnostic algorithms are for specialist use and are not instructions for unsupervised challenge. Asero (PMID 34284571) reports that up to 15 percent of patients with chronic spontaneous urticaria experience severe exacerbations of their baseline cutaneous disease after taking cyclooxygenase-1-inhibiting NSAIDs, and in a study of 235 adults with severe chronic spontaneous urticaria treated with omalizumab found 23 patients (10 percent) hypersensitive to NSAIDs with no difference between the hypersensitive and tolerant groups in disease duration, atopic status, thyroid autoimmunity, C-reactive protein, D-dimer, total immunoglobulin E or the inferred auto-allergic versus autoimmune endotype, concluding that NSAID hypersensitivity in chronic spontaneous urticaria is a phenomenon independent of the pathogenesis of the underlying skin disease. That independence is precisely why the phenotype can be superimposed on any veteran's urticaria and cannot be predicted from the character of the underlying disease. Sánchez and colleagues (PMID 32673879) evaluated 121 patients with chronic spontaneous urticaria and a history of NSAID exacerbations, of whom 96 tested positive on diagnostic challenge and 72 of those (75 percent) tolerated the implicated NSAID when taking H1-antihistamines, which demonstrates both that the exacerbations are reproducible on exposure and that they are dependent on disease control rather than representing fixed permanent intolerance. Framing under 38 CFR § 3.310: this row is a § 3.310(b) aggravation theory. The non-service-connected chronic spontaneous urticaria is the pre-existing baseline and the treatment of the service-connected osteoarthritis is the aggravating factor, so the compensable question is the increase in severity of the urticaria proximately due to the NSAID therapy, and not service connection for urticaria as a whole. Section 3.310(b) permits that increase to be service connected but provides that VA will not concede aggravation unless the baseline level of severity of the non-service-connected disease is established by medical evidence created before the onset of aggravation or by the earliest medical evidence created between the onset of aggravation and the receipt of medical evidence establishing the current level of severity, and the rating activity then determines the baseline and current levels under the rating schedule and deducts the baseline together with any increase due to the natural progress of the disease. The alternative theory must be stated so the row is not misused: if the veteran had no pre-existing urticaria and the drug produced the skin disease de novo, the correct analysis is a § 3.310(a) proximate-result theory of NSAID-induced urticaria or angioedema, which is a different phenotype with a different mechanism and a different evidentiary burden, and this aggravation row must not be pleaded in that posture. Chronology and evidence sufficient for an examiner to conclude that the increase in urticaria severity is at least as likely as not caused by the NSAID therapy prescribed for the service-connected osteoarthritis therefore require: (1) a documented baseline of chronic spontaneous urticaria antedating the claimed aggravation, with contemporaneous records of attack frequency, wheal and angioedema severity, pruritus, functional impact and treatment requirement — an assumption that the skin was previously normal will not do; (2) the exact NSAID agent, dose and dates taken from pharmacy or prescription records, together with documentation that the indication was the service-connected osteoarthritic pain; (3) a comparison of severity before and after the documented exposures, using diaries, photographs, examination findings from both periods and, where available, validated urticaria activity or control scores; and (4) a described latency between dose and flare together with recurrence on subsequent exposure. Four candid limitations belong on the face of the opinion. First, chronic spontaneous urticaria waxes and wanes naturally and can remit for months without any change in exposure, so an increase in symptoms that coincides with NSAID use may be coincidence; the increment must be demonstrated by the before-and-after comparison rather than inferred from proximity in time. Second, tolerance is not fixed: Sánchez and colleagues found that three quarters of previously reactive patients tolerated the implicated NSAID while taking antihistamines, so the opinion must not assert permanent worsening or a permanent intolerance, and the appropriate question is the compensable increase during the relevant period. Third, the opinion must not require or recommend deliberate rechallenge, unsupervised NSAID withdrawal or self-treatment, because diagnostic challenge in this phenotype carries a risk of severe reaction and belongs to specialist care; existing accidental-exposure records or clinically indicated specialist testing are what may be used. Fourth, competing causes that must be excluded or weighed include the natural activity of autoimmune or autoallergic chronic spontaneous urticaria, intercurrent infection, physical or inducible urticaria, other medications, a true single-NSAID immunoglobulin-E-mediated allergy, NSAID-associated food-cofactor reactions and urticarial vasculitis, and lesions that are unusually long-lasting, bruise, or occur with systemic symptoms should trigger diagnostic reassessment rather than forced classification as this phenotype. Rating discipline under § 4.14 and the skin schedule prevents the same wheals or affected skin area from being compensated twice, and the schedule's own definition of chronic urticaria governs whether the condition qualifies at all. No individual probability is asserted here; § 3.102 governs and the opinion must rest on documented chronology, accounted-for competing causes and an approximate balance of evidence.

medicalEvidence.summary: World Allergy Organization statement revising the classification and routine diagnosis of NSAID hypersensitivity, dividing reactions into immediate and delayed and further classifying the immediate reactions into four clinical types including NSAID-exacerbated cutaneous disease, thereby distinguishing that phenotype from NSAID reactions occurring without underlying chronic urticaria and from single-drug immunoglobulin-E-mediated allergy. This is the classification authority that defines the entity and the reason the row is pleaded as aggravation of a pre-existing disease rather than as de novo drug causation.
